content:
When onboarding an advertising data source, the easiest milestone to deliver is “the JSON now matches our common format.” The harder question is whether the transformed record still represents the same business event. A complete set of fields does not make data usable. The first deliverable should be a data contract that can be enforced and reconciled.
This article uses a fictional click-reporting example. It does not describe any company’s internal protocol.
What does one record represent? Suppose a user clicks an ad once, but a response timeout causes the client to deliver the report three times. The ingestion layer receives three requests for one business event. Generating a fresh UUID on every arrival makes those deliveries look like three different events downstream.
Start by distinguishing four identities:
Field Question it answers Suitable for event deduplication? request_id Which ad request? Usually not; one request may contain multiple ad opportunities impression_id Which opportunity or impression, as defined by the protocol? Cannot directly replace a click identifier event_id Which business event? Yes, if its uniqueness scope is explicit delivery_id Which delivery attempt? No; retries should retain the original event_id OpenRTB gives requests, impression objects, and bids their own identities. The auction itself operates at several levels of granularity; one identifier cannot serve as a universal primary key for every downstream event. IAB OpenRTB 2.6 For this design, the deduplication key is (source, event_type, event_id), while delivery_id tracks transport attempts. If a producer has no stable event ID, agree on a deterministic generation rule and document its limits. Concatenating “user + ad + timestamp rounded to a second” can merge two legitimate actions within the same second. That is not a safe default to introduce silently.
Preserve at least two time axes Keep both the business occurrence time, event_time, and the platform receipt time, ingest_time. Processing timestamps can be added, but must not overwrite the original times.
{ "source": "demo-media", "event_type": "click", "event_id": "evt-demo-001", "event_time": "2026-10-01T10:00:00Z", "ingest_time": "2026-10-01T10:00:08Z", "schema_version": "3", "mapping_version": "12" } These values are illustrative. ingest_time - event_time describes arrival delay, but a negative result should not automatically cause a record to be discarded: the client clock may be wrong. Measure negative delays, very late arrivals, and missing timestamps separately. Then apply the contract’s quarantine or correction policy. Store a corrected timestamp in a separate field so that later changes in historical reports remain explainable.
A common event envelope can borrow CloudEvents’ consistent representation of metadata. Business meaning still belongs in the application contract: a standard cannot decide what counts as a valid click. CloudEvents Represent unknown values instead of guessing “Amount missing” and “amount equals zero” are different. So are “user unknown” and “user is an empty string.” Mapping rules should define types, units, null semantics, and handling for unrecognized enum values. For example, represent money as an integer in the currency’s smallest unit and carry the currency separately. Preserve an unfamiliar enum’s original value and mark it unknown instead of mapping it to success.
Versioning also needs separate dimensions: a schema describes the target structure, a mapping describes the source-to-target transformation, and a rule describes a business decision. A mapping that confuses seconds with milliseconds can corrupt the pipeline without changing the schema. Attach all three relevant versions to the output so that replay can reproduce the original result.
I prefer four error categories: unparseable input, missing required identity, invalid business values, and acceptable but incomplete information. The first three go to a quarantine stream. The last may continue with an explicit quality flag. Quarantine needs an owner, a retention policy, and a replay path after repair; it must not become an unmonitored sink for errors.
Acceptance criteria beyond a success rate Build a fixture set covering normal events, duplicate deliveries, out-of-order arrivals, missing IDs, unknown enum values, events crossing a day boundary, oversized fields, and invalid encoding. Then verify the following:
Replaying one event twice produces one business outcome, while the delivery audit retains both attempts. Every input belongs to exactly one category: accepted, intentionally filtered, or quarantined. Their counts add up to the input count. Each target field can be traced to a source field and mapping version. Defaulted values have their own counters. Running old and new mappings on the same fixtures produces differences grouped by field and reason. Monitor delivery volume, valid events, deduplicated events, and successfully joined events separately. A single “success rate” can hide missing IDs behind successful parsing and make retry traffic look like business growth.
The useful artifact is a reviewable contract, fixture set, and error taxonomy—not just a conversion function. Those artifacts make the validation process reusable for the next source.
References IAB Tech Lab: OpenRTB 2.6 , for the boundaries between requests, impression objects, and bids. The event contract here is an independent design example. CloudEvents , for the purpose of consistent event metadata.
description: A duplicate click illustrates the decisions behind event grain, identity, time, versions, and data-quality acceptance criteria.
title: Advertising Event Data: Define the Contract Before Building the Pipeline

content:
When advertising reports disagree, the first reaction is often to investigate data loss. But if one report groups conversions by click date and another by conversion date, their daily totals should differ even when they use identical input. Aligning the comparison before investigating logs saves a great deal of unfocused debugging.
The models and diagnostic steps below are educational examples, not any platform’s billing policy.
Store three kinds of facts separately Consider a user who clicks ad A on Monday, clicks ad B on Tuesday, and makes a payment on Wednesday. The payment is an observed event. Assigning it to B is the output of an attribution rule. Whether it creates a charge, and for how much, depends on a separate billing rule.
These can be represented as three types of records:
Event facts: each click or payment’s event ID, occurrence time, and receipt time. Attribution results: conversion ID, credited touchpoint, weight, model version, and calculation batch. Settlement details: settlement key, currency, amount, rule version, accounting period, and adjustments. This follows the fact-modeling principle of declaring grain first: define the observation represented by one row before choosing dimensions and measures. Copying a payment amount to every touchpoint and then summing it violates that grain. Kimball: Fact Tables For a conversion worth 100 currency units, weights of 0.4 and 0.6 give A and B attributed amounts of 40 and 60. Store the original amount and the weights; do not sum two copies of the original amount into 200. Precision, rounding, and allocation of the remainder must also be defined so the final amounts reconcile.
Define the reconciliation contract before writing SQL An executable reconciliation contract needs at least the data scope, time axis, time zone, conversion window, model version, deduplication key, refund treatment, cutoff time, and rounding precision. Omitting one can turn a difference in definitions into an apparent processing defect.
Google Ads documents differences between reporting by conversion time and by the time of the preceding ad interaction. Even columns with the same business label may use different time semantics. Verify the actual API and column definitions used by an integration. Google Ads: Attribution reports For the example above, I would expose two views. A conversion-date view answers “How many conversions occurred on Wednesday?” A touchpoint-date view answers “How many conversions did Tuesday’s advertising eventually generate?” The first describes business activity; the second evaluates a cohort of advertising activity. They can reconcile over a complete observation period without matching on every day.
Why real-time results need revisions Wednesday’s early report may be missing a payment callback that arrives that afternoon. A refund may arrive on Thursday, followed later by evidence that a touchpoint was invalid. Maintaining only an overwritable aggregate makes these changes difficult to explain.
One traceable design keeps as_of_time and result versions. The event table preserves source facts, the attribution table records the decision at a particular cutoff, and aggregates are generated from a selected version. Externally, distinguish provisional results from closed periods. After closure, record adjustments rather than silently replacing the old result.
A longer window tolerates later data, but increases state, storage, and recomputation costs. There is no universal “seven days is best” setting. Observe callback-delay distributions, then choose a window that also meets the business and contractual requirements. Events beyond that window still need an explicit disposition; closing a window must not erase them from the audit trail.
Drill from aggregate differences down to events My preferred sequence starts by aligning cutoff times, then narrows the comparison:
Compare source inventories, partition completion, and collected record counts to identify incomplete input. Compare pre- and post-deduplication counts, invalid events, and late arrivals to locate filtering differences. Split the delta by source, event date, and event type so positive and negative differences cannot cancel each other out. Full-outer-join the problematic slice by conversion ID. Separate left-only records, right-only records, and shared records with different fields. For shared records, compare touchpoints, weights, window decisions, and rule versions. Difference Next evidence to inspect Present only on the left Raw callback, receipt time, right-side filter reason Different attribution Candidate touchpoints, time zone, model and rule versions Same count, different sum Currency, refunds, weights, precision, rounding The investigation should end with a small set of reproducible examples, not merely “a 0.2% difference.” The same percentage can mean very different risks for a small test campaign and a major settlement period. Acceptance thresholds should consider absolute record counts, money, and critical sources. Every accepted discrepancy needs an explanation.
References Ralph Kimball: Fact Tables , on consistent fact grain and measures. Google Ads: About attribution reports , on attribution reports, standard reports, and time semantics. Platform policies can change.
description: A conversion spanning several days explains event facts, attribution results, metric definitions, and systematic reconciliation.
title: Ad Attribution and Reconciliation: Why Two Correct Reports Can Disagree

content:
One source sends Kafka messages, another writes object-storage files, and a third calls an HTTP endpoint. Their payloads may be JSON, CSV, or Protobuf. Copying a job for each source is quick at first, until a timestamp bug needs to be fixed in a dozen branches. A more maintainable approach shares the processing core and contains source differences in adapters and mapping rules.
Moving behavior into configuration does not remove the need for software releases. One incorrect configuration line can affect an entire batch of events. The following is a reference design.
Share processing semantics, not source cursors Split the pipeline into read → decode → map → validate → enrich → write. Each stage should return a result or a structured error, with minimal direct manipulation of source offsets. Offline replay and streaming consumption can then use the same mapping and validation logic.
The reader must retain its own progress semantics. Kafka uses partitions and offsets; a file reader needs object identity, version, and record position. Collapsing these into an ambiguous lastPosition loses useful guarantees. For example, S3 event notifications use at-least-once delivery. A repeated notification is not a new file, so file processing needs its own idempotency record. AWS S3 Event Notifications A practical source envelope can contain source_id, a source locator, read time, a digest of the raw payload, and a parser version. The digest helps with lookup and verification; it does not replace controlled retention of the original input. Sensitive raw payloads should stay out of ordinary error logs.
Treat mapping rules with the rigor of code source: demo_partner mapping_version: 12 fields: event_id: from: $.tracking.id required: true event_time: from: $.timestamp transform: epoch_millis_to_utc amount_minor: from: $.price transform: decimal_major_to_minor currency_from: $.currency This illustrative configuration makes units and conversion functions explicit. Avoid arbitrary script execution, and do not turn every failure into a null. At load time, check field paths, target types, enum values, and transformation parameters. At execution time, record the specific rule that failed.
Java’s DynamicMessage can represent message types using a Descriptor, reducing the need to regenerate and release code whenever a target structure changes. It addresses structural representation, however; it does not automatically provide correct mappings, thread safety, or lossless rollback. Protobuf DynamicMessage Package the Descriptor, mapping, and validation rules into an immutable version. An event should use one snapshot throughout its processing. Otherwise, a hot update can cause the first half of the event’s processing to use old rules and the second half to use new ones.
Test compatibility and business meaning separately Deleted Protobuf field numbers must not be casually reused. Even wire-compatible changes can violate business meaning: changing an amount from cents to whole currency units while keeping the same integer type introduces a hundredfold error downstream. Protobuf proto3 guide I would maintain a small, stable contract fixture set for each source: normal input, missing fields, invalid types, unknown fields, boundary amounts, time-zone differences, duplicate records, and historical versions. After structural validation, check business assertions such as amount ranges, event times, required IDs, and output enums.
An LLM can suggest field mappings or additional test cases, but its suggestions should not directly replace production rules. The useful output is a candidate mapping, supporting evidence, and unresolved questions, followed by deterministic validation and a diff. If the source unit is unclear, an unresolved result is more reliable than a plausible guess.
Releases need traceability and a way back Before release, process a controlled sample with both versions and compare parsing rates, defaulted values, event distributions, and field-level differences. Use source-based or stable-hash cohorts for staged rollout so retries of one event do not randomly receive different rules. Record the rule version on every output to identify the results affected by a problem.
Rolling back a configuration changes future processing; it does not repair incorrect data already written. A release record also needs the impact scope, replayable source locations, downstream idempotency keys, and a repair plan. Before promising one-click replay, demonstrate that repeating an external write cannot double-charge or double-count.
After onboarding, slice quality dashboards by source and version. A small source’s missing-required-field rate can climb from zero to ten percent with almost no visible effect on global success rates. Alongside percentages, show absolute error counts, first-seen times, and sanitized sample locations to help identify the upstream change.
Acceptance testing should deliberately simulate three failures: a partially loaded configuration, an object overwritten during processing, and a process exit after successful output. Verify atomic version switching, object identity checks, and replay idempotency respectively. Configuration reduces maintenance costs when the system can explain and handle these boundaries.
References AWS S3 Event Notifications , for at-least-once notification semantics. Protobuf DynamicMessage Java API , for Descriptor-based message handling. Protobuf proto3 Language Guide , for field numbers, reserved fields, and evolution constraints.
description: A shared ingestion core for JSON, CSV, and Protobuf, with explicit boundaries for dynamic mapping, replay, and staged releases.
title: Heterogeneous Ad Data Ingestion: Configuration Still Needs a Release Process

content:
Deduplication needs a more precise definition than “drop this ID if we have seen it.” Whose ID is it? How long do we remember it? Does the guarantee span jobs? After a crash, are duplicates acceptable, or is loss acceptable? This article uses Flink 1.15 DataStream as its baseline and discusses exact deduplication within a finite retention period.
Write down the business boundary first Suppose a producer guarantees that event_id is unique within its source and duplicates arrive no more than a day late. (source, event_id) is a possible logical key. But should replaying a week-old input count as a duplicate? A one-day TTL cannot provide deduplication across an arbitrary historical range.
Estimate capacity before implementation. At 100,000 unique events per second and one day of retention, there are about 8.64 billion active keys. Even an assumed 32 bytes per key gives roughly 276 GB in decimal units, before serialization, indexes, timestamps, and backend overhead. This is an order-of-magnitude example, not a production benchmark.
Keyed State: recover state with the job For a single Flink pipeline, keyBy on the complete deduplication key and one seen flag per key is often the most direct design. Once checkpointed, source positions and deduplication state can recover consistently. End-to-end exactly-once output still depends on the sink’s transaction or idempotency protocol.
onEvent(event): if seen.value() is absent: seen.update(true) emit(event) This pseudocode describes only the decision. In Flink 1.15, State TTL is based on processing time. Visibility of expired values, TTL refresh behavior, and background cleanup are separate choices. Logical expiration does not immediately shrink state files. Flink 1.15: Working with State If the contract requires event-time retention, design time buckets and timers explicitly, including stalled watermarks, late data, and bucket boundaries. Processing-time TTL is not an event-time window. Retention planning must also account for records replayed after recovery, the latest permitted arrival, and clock boundaries.
Redis: shared decisions introduce an external consistency problem Redis is convenient when several services need a shared deduplication decision. SET key 1 NX EX 86400 combines conditional insertion and expiration in one command, avoiding a separate check-then-write race. Redis SET An atomic Redis command does not atomically complete business processing:
The Redis write succeeds. The job crashes before sending the event downstream. Recovery replays the event, finds the Redis marker, and drops it. This failure window can lose the business outcome. Reversing the order can create duplicate output, so ordering must be designed together with the recovery protocol. If reliable delivery happens before recording completion, the sink needs event-key idempotency to absorb retries before the completion marker is written. If the design reserves the event first, persist distinct pending and completed states, then retry delivery or reconcile after recovery. Pending must not be treated as completed and discarded.
Adding an idempotent sink alone does not repair the loss window above: the event never reached the sink. Calling a Redis key “completed” requires evidence of completion, not merely receipt.
Also decide what happens on a Redis timeout: block, quarantine, or allow processing. Unbounded retries can amplify tail latency; allowing processing weakens deduplication; dropping the event risks data loss. The choice depends on the data’s use. Billing events and exploratory metrics should not inherit the same policy by accident.
Bitmap: compression does not solve identity RoaringBitmap represents integer sets and uses compressed representations suited to different distributions. Its memory benefit depends on the distribution of IDs, not just their count. RoaringBitmap repository When input already has stable, collision-free integer IDs, time-bucketed bitmaps can be useful. Hashing strings into 32-bit integers introduces collisions and may classify distinct events as duplicates. A longer hash reduces the probability; it does not make the mapping mathematically exact. Strict use cases need collision-free mapping or a secondary verification step.
Daily buckets also create a midnight boundary: a retry today may refer to yesterday’s event. Query the buckets required by the business retention interval, then delete those no longer needed. Coarse buckets retain data longer; fine buckets increase metadata, lookup, and serialization overhead.
Choose a design and test its guarantees Approach Useful starting point Critical checks Keyed State Deduplication within one job Checkpoint recovery, TTL, state capacity Redis Shared deduplication across pipelines External-write failure windows, timeouts, availability Bitmap Integer ID sets and bulk set operations Identity mapping, ID distribution, bucket boundaries Load tests should go beyond steady-state throughput. Include hot sources, duplicate bursts, replay beyond retention, state recovery, and sink failures. For correctness, use a known set of unique events and count duplicate and missing outputs separately. For performance, measure processing latency, checkpoint size, recovery time, and external request volume together.
When approaches behave differently under failure, first choose one that meets the delivery contract, then optimize its cost. An incorrectly discarded legitimate event is harder to spot in a report than a slightly larger state footprint.
References Flink 1.15: State and TTL . Redis: SET command . RoaringBitmap implementation and documentation .
description: Compare deduplication scope, recovery semantics, capacity, and the failure windows hidden inside three common approaches.
title: Real-Time Deduplication in Flink: State, Redis, or Bitmap?

content:
A Flink job starting after an upgrade proves that the new program can run. It does not prove that all old state was restored or that output semantics are unchanged. Migration acceptance needs three independent forms of evidence: recoverable state, correct business results, and acceptable operational behavior.
This article discusses migration to Flink 1.15 as a baseline. When crossing several versions, check the compatibility notes for each runtime and connector. “We use a savepoint” is not a guarantee that any two versions support a direct upgrade.
Freeze what you are comparing Combining a runtime upgrade, business-logic changes, schema changes, and a source migration in one release makes differences difficult to explain. Separate them when practical. If they must ship together, define an expected result for each category of change.
A migration inventory should include Flink and Java versions, connector versions, operator UIDs, state names, serializers, key types, maximum parallelism, checkpoint settings, time zones, external dependency versions, and sink semantics. Many apparent runtime-upgrade failures are actually changed defaults or dependency conflicts.
Flink savepoints associate state with operator identity. The documentation recommends explicit UIDs to reduce the effect of topology changes on automatically generated identifiers. Flink 1.15: Savepoints Stable UIDs are only one requirement. Whether a state-field change is compatible depends on the serializer. Changes to a key’s schema in particular cannot be treated as ordinary field evolution. Flink 1.15: State Schema Evolution Share facts between parallel runs, not side effects The old and new jobs should read the same logical input interval and write to isolated result sets. Kafka consumers can use separate groups with aligned partition boundaries. File replay should use a frozen inventory and object versions. A shadow job must not trigger duplicate charges, notifications, or irreversible writes.
External dimension data is an easily missed variable. If the old job reads user label X in the morning and the new job reads Y in the afternoon, identical code can still produce different results. Freeze dimension snapshots, record external responses, or pin versions during validation. When that is impossible, track these nondeterministic fields separately instead of attributing every difference to the upgrade.
Make the warm-up boundary explicit as well. A new job starting with empty deduplication state, windows, and caches will naturally differ from a long-running job. Use comparable initial state, or identify a warm-up interval and compare only an adequately covered event range.
Move from record-level diffs to business meaning First compare accounting identities: inputs, filtered records, errors, and outputs. Next compare sets by business key. Only then compare fields on records present on both sides.
left_only Present in the old pipeline, absent in the new one right_only Present in the new pipeline, absent in the old one field_diff The same business key has different field values duplicate One side contains multiple records for a business key Detect duplicates before joining; otherwise a many-to-many join can inflate differences. Compare nested maps by their key-value meaning. Apply floating-point tolerances only where the business permits them. Maintain an explicit ignore list for nonbusiness fields such as processing timestamps and trace IDs. Do not hide every inconvenient difference behind an unexplained regular expression.
For windowed aggregates, compare results for settled windows, not two arbitrary live snapshots. Align the event-time interval, watermark progress, late-data handling, and final-result version. Matching overall totals is insufficient: an increase in one source can cancel a decrease in another.
Verify recovery before cutover and retain repair options afterward Run at least one rehearsal of “restore the new version from the intended state → process controlled input → fail and recover again.” Inspect timers, deduplication state, and external writes. Before enabling an option that allows unrestored state, identify exactly what would be abandoned. It should not be a generic switch for making startup turn green.
The acceptance report can be short, but its evidence must be traceable:
Dimension Evidence Correctness Comparison interval, sample size, difference categories, explanations State Savepoint restoration outcome and assertions on critical state Performance Latency, backlog, CPU, state size, and checkpoints under comparable load Recovery Time to recover from an injected failure; duplicate and missing event counts Rollback Old artifacts, recoverable state, input retention, and treatment of external output Rolling back the runtime does not undo records already written by the new version. Design idempotency keys or repair batches before migration, and verify that the old version can read the state intended for rollback. Treating rollback as “deploy the old package again” misses its hardest part.
References Flink 1.15: Savepoints , for operator UIDs and restoration behavior. Flink 1.15: State Schema Evolution , for serialization compatibility constraints.
description: Separate state compatibility, result correctness, and performance regressions to make streaming migrations diagnosable and reversible.
title: Upgrading Flink Jobs: Turn Parallel Runs and Diffs into Evidence

content:
When Kafka backlog rises and checkpoints time out, increasing parallelism is rarely the most informative first step. If a downstream service is throttling requests, more concurrency may amplify failures and retries. Separate “where is it slow?” from “why is it slow?” before choosing a setting to change.
This article uses Flink 1.15 and the illustrative pipeline Source → Parse → Enrich → Keyed Process → Sink. Any performance numbers are hypothetical examples.
The backpressured task is not necessarily the bottleneck Records move downstream; backpressure propagates upstream. A backpressured Source often means downstream capacity is restricting its output, not that the Source itself is too slow. Flink’s Web UI exposes busy, idle, and backpressure time metrics for inspecting parallel task instances. Flink 1.15: Monitoring Back Pressure Work upstream from the downstream end to locate the blocking boundary, and inspect individual subtasks. If fifteen Process instances are relatively idle while one stays busy, examine key distribution first. If all are busy with high CPU use, inspect computation and serialization. If CPU is low but request latency is high, investigate external waits and connection pools.
Operator chaining can place several functions in one task, so one graph node does not necessarily equal one business stage. If needed, break the chain in a controlled environment or add per-stage timing. Otherwise reflection-based parsing, network calls, and business computation may all disappear into a single busy metric.
Preserve evidence before running a controlled experiment A useful snapshot includes input rate and backlog trends, per-subtask input and output volumes, CPU and GC behavior, external-request latency and errors, state size, and checkpoint-stage durations. Record when the issue began and the most recent release, traffic change, or dependency change.
Suppose the dimension service used by Enrich suddenly has higher tail latency. Test whether reducing external calls relieves backpressure: in an isolated environment, substitute a fixed response or controlled cache while keeping input unchanged. If the problem improves, investigate timeouts, concurrency limits, cache hit rates, and retries. An unbounded production queue does not solve a slow dependency; it converts delay into a memory risk.
For skew, measure load by key or business partition. Salting may spread a hot key, but can change aggregation, deduplication, and ordering semantics. It needs a subsequent merge or a deliberate hot-key strategy, not a random suffix added indiscriminately to every key.
Break checkpoint duration into stages A slow checkpoint can result from delayed barrier arrival, alignment across inputs, blocking synchronous snapshot work, or slow asynchronous upload. Combine subtask-level metrics rather than relying on one end-to-end duration.
Observation Hypothesis to investigate first Start delay and alignment rise with backlog Backpressure is delaying barrier propagation Synchronous duration suddenly increases More expensive state serialization or synchronous work Asynchronous duration and storage latency increase Checkpoint-storage I/O bottleneck A few subtasks hold much larger state Key skew, excessive retention, or ineffective cleanup These are investigative starting points, not proof of causation. A jump in state size may come from higher traffic or from a deduplication-key change that increases cardinality. Compare state trends with unique-key counts, TTL settings, and release history.
Which problem do unaligned checkpoints address? Under severe backpressure, unaligned checkpoints include some in-flight data in the snapshot so barriers need not wait for all buffered records to be processed. This adds storage I/O. If snapshot-upload bandwidth is already the bottleneck, it may not help. Flink 1.15: Checkpointing under backpressure Flink 1.15 also imposes configuration constraints, including exactly-once checkpoints and a single concurrent checkpoint. Flink 1.15: Checkpointing I would evaluate this as a conditional experiment under the same input load. Compare checkpoint success rate, size, end-to-end latency, and actual recovery time after a failure. Declaring success solely because checkpoints stop timing out can overlook the volume of in-flight data that recovery must read.
What counts as a completed fix? After a change, observe at least a traffic peak and one recovery exercise. Confirm that backlog drains rather than merely stops growing. Successful downstream writes must keep pace, and the volume of quarantined errors must not quietly increase.
If scaling is the final choice, state whether it addresses CPU, state capacity, or throughput. Check whether source partitions, hot keys, or external rate limits constrain the benefit. A useful incident conclusion is concrete: “Dependency tail latency increased waiting; after bounding retries and improving cache hits, backlog began to drain under controlled load.” “Tuning made a big difference” is not enough.
Keep the configurations and observation windows from before and after the change. A temporary traffic drop can make an ineffective change appear successful, so compare similar input volumes and event distributions. Average latency can hide the tail; also inspect high-percentile latency and the age of the oldest queued event.
References Flink 1.15: Monitoring Back Pressure . Flink 1.15: Checkpointing under backpressure . Flink 1.15: Checkpointing .
description: Use a source-to-sink pipeline to distinguish downstream bottlenecks, data skew, state I/O, and barrier-alignment delays.
title: Debugging Flink Backpressure and Checkpoints: Locate the Slow Stage First

content:
Scope: MySQL 8.0 / InnoDB. EXPLAIN ANALYZE requires 8.0.18 or later. The examples are illustrative and contain no production data or benchmark claims.
Slow-query optimization often goes wrong when type=ALL immediately triggers a new index, or a nonempty key field is treated as proof of success. The useful questions are how much data the database reads, how much it sorts to return a few dozen rows, and what the chosen index costs on the write path.
Start with the complete query requirement Suppose an administrative page needs the latest 50 click events for an account after a specified time. Ordering by both event_time and id makes the order deterministic when timestamps are equal:
CREATE TABLE event_log ( id BIGINT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, account_id BIGINT NOT NULL, event_type VARCHAR(16) NOT NULL, event_time DATETIME(3) NOT NULL, payload JSON, KEY idx_account_type_time (account_id, event_type, event_time, id) ) ENGINE=InnoDB; SELECT id, event_time FROM event_log WHERE account_id = 42 AND event_type = 'click' AND event_time >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00' ORDER BY event_time DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50; This index order is a hypothesis to validate: constrain the account and event type, then search the time range. The queries a composite index can serve depend on column order and predicates; a composite index is not simply a collection of single-column indexes. See the MySQL documentation on multiple-column indexes for the leftmost-prefix rules.
Other queries need their own analysis. An endpoint filtering only by event_type across all accounts has a different access pattern. Conversely, if nearly every event for an account is a click, event_type may contribute little filtering. Whether to retain it also depends on other queries, index width, and write frequency.
Read the plan as a set of questions Start with ordinary EXPLAIN to inspect the access path and estimated scan volume. Then run the following in a controlled environment:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT id, event_time FROM event_log WHERE account_id = 42 AND event_type = 'click' AND event_time >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00' ORDER BY event_time DESC, id DESC LIMIT 50; EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement and reports actual rows, timing, and loop counts. For an inner nested-loop operation, per-loop timing alone understates the total work. Parent and child timings must not be added mechanically either, because a parent’s execution includes its children. The version requirements and output semantics are documented in EXPLAIN .
I follow four questions through the execution tree: How much did the index narrow the candidate set? How many candidates were filtered out? How many rows were sorted? Did LIMIT stop the read early enough? When estimates and actuals diverge, I check parameter distributions, statistics, and skew before considering optimizer hints.
Using filesort indicates an additional sorting step; it does not by itself mean the sort spilled to disk. Whether an index can provide the required order also depends on the query. Judge the cost using row counts and actual time, as described in ORDER BY optimization .
Validate against the data distribution One execution for an average account is insufficient. Include large accounts, small accounts, accounts with no results, and both narrow and wide time windows. A fast run against a warm cache does not establish cold-start or concurrent-read performance.
If the page also needs payload, do not put every field into an index merely to make it covering. Compare direct clustered-index lookups with fetching 50 primary keys and then loading the details. The latter adds a query and introduces consistency questions if data changes between the two reads. Add that complexity only when measurements identify row lookups as a significant cost.
Deep pagination needs a separate design. OFFSET 100000 asks the database to skip many results. Cursor pagination can return the last timestamp and ID and continue with a strict less-than predicate. This requires stable ordering keys and an explicit product decision about the visibility of inserts and deletes between pages.
Make the optimization reviewable Keep the original SQL, representative parameters, table and index definitions, before-and-after plans, scan volumes, and latency percentiles under comparable load. Include write throughput, index size, and replication lag so that read improvements do not conceal regressions on the write path.
After rollout, monitor query digests rather than a single manually executed statement. Keep a rollback path if the benefit is unstable, and determine whether data distribution, plan selection, lock waits, or I/O explains the difference. A useful index optimization ends with an access-path decision supported by evidence.
References MySQL 8.0: Multiple-Column Indexes MySQL 8.0: EXPLAIN Statement MySQL 8.0: ORDER BY Optimization

content:
Scope: MySQL 8.0 / InnoDB. The examples use explicit transactions and assume REPEATABLE READ unless stated otherwise. Run the experiments in an isolated test database.
The claim that “MVCC prevents read/write conflicts” is only partly true. Consistent nonlocking reads, locking reads, and modification statements use different mechanisms. Mixing them up can produce code that works with one client but oversells inventory or blocks for a long time under concurrency.
A snapshot does not enforce a business invariant Start with a small test table:
CREATE TABLE inventory ( sku_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, available INT NOT NULL ) ENGINE=InnoDB; INSERT INTO inventory VALUES (1, 10), (2, 10); Session A starts a transaction and performs an ordinary read of sku_id=1. Session B updates that row and commits. A then repeats its ordinary read. Under REPEATABLE READ, A generally sees the old value through the same consistent snapshot. Under READ COMMITTED, each consistent read establishes a new snapshot. A transaction’s own changes introduce visibility exceptions, so a snapshot is not simply a frozen copy of the entire database. See consistent nonlocking reads .
If the application reads inventory, subtracts one locally, and writes the computed value back, two requests can start from the same old value. For a single-row decrement, putting the condition and change in one statement is clearer:
UPDATE inventory SET available = available - 1 WHERE sku_id = 1 AND available > 0; The application checks the affected-row count: one means the decrement succeeded; zero means no qualifying row was available. If the operation also changes an order or a quota, it still needs a complete transaction. Repeated business requests need a unique constraint or another idempotency mechanism.
The access path determines what gets locked InnoDB record locks apply to index records. Range access can also involve gap locks and next-key locks. A lookup of one unique value through a unique index does not have the same locking footprint as a range scan using nonunique conditions. The mechanisms are described in InnoDB Locking .
When two requests update different business objects but still block each other, I first collect the actual SQL, parameters, isolation level, and execution plan. Without a suitable index, a narrow business condition can lead to a much broader scan and locking footprint. I also check for network calls inside the transaction: locks may already be held while the application waits for an external service.
Reproduce a deadlock with two sessions Execute the following steps in order. The last step closes the wait cycle:
Step Session A Session B 1 BEGIN; BEGIN; 2 Update sku_id=1 Update sku_id=2 3 Update sku_id=2; wait for B No action yet 4 Still waiting Update sku_id=1; wait for A With deadlock detection enabled, as it is by default, InnoDB chooses a victim transaction to roll back so that the other can proceed. A deadlock and a lock wait timeout are different events. In particular, a lock wait timeout must not be assumed to roll back the entire transaction. After an error, end the current transaction according to the driver and transaction manager’s semantics before deciding whether to retry.
After reproducing the issue, inspect:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS; SELECT * FROM performance_schema.data_lock_waits; The first exposes information about the latest deadlock; the second helps inspect current wait relationships. A relationship may disappear as soon as the wait ends, so retain the SQL, transaction IDs, and timestamps from the incident. See the official data_lock_waits definition .
Retry the business transaction A direct way to reduce deadlocks is to acquire resources in a consistent order across entry points. For example, sort SKU IDs before updating multiple inventory rows. Keep transactions short, perform calculations that do not depend on locks beforehand, and index the filtering conditions appropriately. These measures do not eliminate all deadlocks; applications must still handle retries, as the official deadlock guidance explains.
Retry the complete business transaction. Retrying only its final failed statement does not restore earlier changes that were rolled back. Bound the number of attempts, use randomized backoff, and return a clear error when the overall deadline is exhausted. Side effects outside the database transaction, such as sending messages or calling a payment service, require idempotency keys or a transactional messaging design before they can safely be repeated.
Validation should check more than an improved success rate. Inventory must remain nonnegative, orders and decrements must correspond, and failed requests must not leave transactions open. Business invariants provide the evidence that concurrency control works.
References MySQL 8.0: Consistent Nonlocking Reads MySQL 8.0: InnoDB Locking MySQL 8.0: How to Minimize and Handle Deadlocks MySQL 8.0: data_lock_waits
description: Use two sessions to understand snapshot reads and conflicting updates, inspect deadlocks, and design retries at the transaction boundary.
title: MySQL Concurrency: MVCC, Lock Waits, and Deadlocks in One Example

content:
Scope: the concepts and documented semantics of MySQL 8.0, Debezium 2.7, and Kafka 3.9. This is a design discussion, not a production configuration checklist.
Getting database changes into a message queue is usually the easy part. Recovery exposes the harder questions: What happens when an update arrives twice? Can changes made during a snapshot be missed? Could a late, older update recreate an object that has already been deleted?
Distinguish three kinds of position The source binlog position, the offset persisted by the connector, and the downstream Kafka consumer offset answer different questions. They are not interchangeable, and progress in any one of them does not prove that the business result is correct.
Debezium’s initial snapshot establishes a baseline before streaming changes from the log. Recovery can repeat events. If the binlog history needed for recovery has already been purged, the connector cannot reconstruct it from nothing. Snapshot and failure behavior should be checked for the selected mode in the Debezium 2.7 MySQL connector documentation .
Operational planning therefore needs the source-log retention window, maximum tolerable downtime, connector lag, downstream backlog, and the time required to rebuild a baseline. A seven-day binlog retention setting is only a configuration value until a recovery exercise demonstrates what it actually supports.
Identify the entity and the change separately For an order-state table, a normalized change event might look like this:
{ "entity_key": "order:1001", "event_id": "source-a:tx-17:row-2", "version": 12, "operation": "upsert", "value": {"status": "PAID"} } This is an illustrative format. event_id must come from a real, stable event-identity rule. version represents a monotonically increasing version maintained explicitly by the upstream application; it is not a universal sequence number supplied by Debezium. A binlog filename or timestamp cannot be assumed to provide a total order across failover, snapshot rebuilding, and multiple sources.
For a sink that stores the latest state, define the rules explicitly: a higher version replaces a lower one; the same version with identical content is a replay; the same version with different content is a conflict to investigate; and lower versions are ignored and counted. The comparison and write must be atomic, or concurrent consumers can still overwrite state incorrectly.
For an aggregate that increments on every change, overwriting by entity key is insufficient. Record processed event IDs and commit the deduplication record and aggregate update in the same transaction, or use a processing system that can commit state and progress together. The deduplication retention period must cover the possible replay window. Replaying after those records expire can cause duplicate increments again.
Deletes and reordering need explicit rules Physically deleting a target row also removes its version. A later replay of an old update can then insert the row again. One option is to retain a logical deletion marker with its version until the replay boundary has passed. This application-level deletion marker is different from a null-valued tombstone in a compacted Kafka topic.
Also cover primary-key changes, snapshot read events, schema changes, and parsing failures. Silently skipping an unreadable field can make lag look healthy while the sink is missing rows. When isolating failed events, retain sanitized context, error classification, and source position so the data can be replayed after a fix.
Kafka transactions do not close every boundary Kafka transactions can coordinate output records and consumer positions within Kafka. Writing to an external database, search index, or HTTP service requires cooperation from the destination. The boundary is described in Kafka 3.9 message delivery semantics .
For example, the destination database may commit successfully just before the consumer crashes, before its Kafka offset is committed. On recovery, the consumer reads the same event again. A version-conditional, idempotent write can prevent that replay from creating an additional business effect. Committing the offset before writing to the database creates the opposite failure window: progress is recorded, but the result is absent.
Validate with a failure matrix I prefer the following experiments to a single comparison of total row counts:
Failure or disturbance Expected result Repeatedly update one key during a snapshot Final state matches the source; the snapshot-to-log transition has no gap Terminate the consumer immediately after the sink commits Replay does not double-count or repeat side effects Replay an older update after a delete The deleted entity stays deleted Deliver changes for one key out of order A lower version cannot replace a higher version Add a field or change a field type Compatibility rules or a recoverable isolation workflow handle the change Finally, reconcile counts, important fields, and deletion state by primary-key range, and retain a small sample of row-level differences. Equal total counts cannot expose a missing row canceled out by a duplicate elsewhere. A dependable CDC pipeline must let an operator explain, recover, and reconcile business-state changes after a failure.
References Debezium 2.7: MySQL Connector, Snapshots, Change Events, and Failure Handling Apache Kafka 3.9: Message Delivery Semantics
description: Trace duplicates, reordering, deletes, and replay from MySQL through Debezium and Kafka to downstream state.
title: Consistency Boundaries in MySQL CDC: Snapshots, Offsets, and Idempotency

Scope: Java 17 platform threads and ThreadPoolExecutor. Java 21 virtual threads are outside this article. Capacity numbers are illustrative, not recommended settings.
A thread pool makes the amount of concurrent work a system is willing to accept explicit. When downstream processing is slower than incoming work, a backlog is inevitable. The design determines whether that backlog accumulates in an in-memory queue, at the caller, in a message broker, or becomes an explicit rejection.
A queue does not create throughput Suppose an external call occupies a worker for 20 milliseconds on average, with an average arrival rate of 500 calls per second. Under stable conditions, the average in-flight requirement is approximately 10 calls. That is only a starting estimate: it excludes tail latency, retries, bursts, and downstream capacity. It does not establish that 10 threads are sufficient.
If downstream latency rises to 200 milliseconds, maintaining the same throughput requires more concurrency. Adding workers, however, may further overload the dependency. If the service continues accepting everything, the queue absorbs the difference until waiting time exceeds request deadlines. The system then spends effort on requests whose callers have already given up.
Capacity design needs at least two budgets: how many tasks may execute concurrently, and how many may wait. Record enqueue time, check the remaining deadline before execution, and discard expired work when its business semantics permit that.
Make the boundary visible The following fragment belongs in service initialization. Its types come from java.util.concurrent; worker count and queue capacity must be validated against the actual workload:
ThreadPoolExecutor ioPool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 16, 16, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(256), Executors.defaultThreadFactory(), new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy() ); try { ioPool.execute(task); } catch (RejectedExecutionException overloaded) { // Record the rejection at ingress and return a recognizable overload result. // Do not retry indefinitely here or silently lose reliable messages. throw overloaded; } Queue behavior affects ThreadPoolExecutor growth. Once the core worker count is reached, it generally tries to enqueue before adding workers up to the maximum. An unbounded queue can therefore prevent maximumPoolSize from providing the limit or scaling behavior the author expected. See the ThreadPoolExecutor contract .
ArrayBlockingQueue bounds the number of queued tasks. Using a blocking queue does not mean that submitting work to the executor necessarily blocks: the executor’s submission path differs from calling the queue’s put method directly. See ArrayBlockingQueue .
Match rejection behavior to the entry point An HTTP endpoint can return a recognizable overload response with a documented retry policy. A reliable message consumer may need to pause fetching or reduce concurrency. Acknowledging a message after its task is rejected turns a capacity problem into data loss. A recovery queue also needs limits, retention, and monitoring; otherwise it merely moves an unbounded backlog elsewhere.
CallerRunsPolicy is often used for backpressure: the submitting thread executes the task and consequently submits more slowly. That consumes the caller’s thread. If it also handles an event loop, heartbeats, or consumer coordination, the impact can spread. The policy also discards rejected tasks when the executor has been shut down, as documented in CallerRunsPolicy . It is not a universally safe default.
With multiple dependencies, isolating execution resources by dependency often makes failures easier to contain. A slow query service should not exhaust the threads required for heartbeats or critical responses. Isolation can leave capacity idle when pools cannot share it, so the tradeoff depends on traffic and priority.
Measure waiting separately from execution Thread count and CPU usage miss important failure modes. Track queue wait time, execution time, active workers, queue depth, rejections, expired tasks, and latency and errors by dependency. When end-to-end latency rises, determine whether the extra time is spent waiting or executing.
Queue memory is not simply the number of tasks multiplied by request-body size. A closure may retain large objects, context, buffers, or a whole batch. Inspect what queued tasks retain. Increasing queue capacity tenfold can increase both tail latency and heap occupancy.
Test overload and recovery Include three phases in validation: stable traffic, a sudden input increase, and an injected downstream slowdown followed by recovery. Check that rejection occurs at the intended boundary, the system recovers, and upstream retries do not amplify rejections into a storm. Also simulate shutdown and verify the policy for refusing new work and finishing or recovering accepted tasks.
A sound outcome has controlled latency within capacity, explicit failure beyond capacity, a backlog that drains after recovery, and a defined replay path for reliable data.
References Java SE 17: ThreadPoolExecutor Java SE 17: ArrayBlockingQueue Java SE 17: CallerRunsPolicy
description: Use worker, queue, and rejection limits to control how bursts turn into latency and memory pressure, then validate overload behavior.
title: Java Thread-Pool Capacity: Keeping Backpressure Under Control

content:
Scope: HotSpot JDK 17, with G1 as the garbage-collector example. Replace the example PID 12345 before running commands. In containers, also verify PID namespaces and diagnostic-tool permissions.
“The endpoint is slow, so increase the heap” is an expensive guess. Latency may come from queueing, lock contention, networking, CPU throttling, or garbage collection. The first task is to distinguish those explanations.
Capture evidence from the same time window Record incident onset, deployed version, request volume, error rate, latency percentiles, and dependency latency. Inspect process CPU, memory, container limits, and disk at the same time. Comparing a GC chart with request and host metrics from a different period makes false causal explanations easy to construct.
Then establish the runtime environment:
jcmd 12345 VM.version jcmd 12345 VM.flags jcmd 12345 GC.heap_info jcmd 12345 Thread.print -l Use jcmd 12345 help to check supported commands and review their impact before running them. The commands are documented in JDK 17 jcmd . A command working on a development machine does not establish that it is available inside a production container.
When CPU is high, locate the work High CPU may reflect more business computation, serialization, regular expressions, busy waiting, or GC. A thread stack offers a clue, but one snapshot can land in incidental code. Repeated occurrences of the same stack, supported by CPU sampling, are stronger evidence.
During an appropriate diagnostic window, a short JFR recording can help:
jcmd 12345 JFR.start name=incident settings=profile duration=60s filename=/tmp/incident.jfr Inspect hot stacks, locks, allocations, and I/O events, then connect them back to the request path. The profile configuration adds overhead and should first be evaluated in a comparable environment. Store recordings somewhere with enough capacity and controlled access. See the JDK diagnostic tools guide for JFR capabilities and operation.
An application may also lack CPU time even when process CPU looks modest, because the container is being throttled. Adding threads can intensify that competition. Read process metrics alongside host conditions and container quotas.
When CPU is low but latency is high, inspect waits Determine whether threads are waiting for database connections, HTTP connections, locks, queues, or futures that never complete. Then inspect utilization and waiting time for the corresponding resource.
If workers are waiting for a connection pool whose connections are occupied by slow SQL, increasing workers from 32 to 128 will not make the database finish more queries. It adds waiters. The fix must address the actual bottleneck: query performance, connection hold time, or dependency capacity.
Also inspect dependencies between tasks in the same executor. A task that submits a child task to a saturated pool and then waits synchronously for it can cause thread starvation. A diagram of who is waiting for whom is more useful than a count of threads in WAITING state.
Rising memory is not automatically a heap leak Heap occupancy normally rises within a GC cycle. The more useful questions are whether post-GC live data keeps growing under comparable traffic and which objects remain reachable. Unbounded caches, queues, and unregistered listeners can all produce growth that follows the code’s logic but violates its capacity assumptions.
Process RSS also includes direct memory, thread stacks, metaspace, and other native allocations. If the heap is stable while the process grows, extend the investigation to those areas. Native Memory Tracking can compare a baseline with later measurements when enabled at startup. It does not account for every third-party native allocation, so it is not a complete RSS ledger.
A heap dump can expose retention paths, but collection may cause pauses, consume substantial disk space, and capture business data. Collect one when it is needed to answer a specific question and capacity is available. Lower-cost observations should narrow the hypothesis first.
Tune GC for a confirmed problem For G1, record pause causes and frequency, allocation rate, post-GC live data, and large-object behavior. The pause target is a tuning objective, not a hard latency guarantee. The official guidance recommends starting with defaults and an appropriate heap limit, then tuning for observed behavior: G1 Tuning .
Change one major variable at a time and compare throughput, tail latency, CPU, and memory under similar load. Changing heap size, GC settings, executors, and connection pools together makes an improvement difficult to explain and the next incident harder to diagnose.
A useful incident record connects the symptom and its timing, the evidence that ruled out alternatives, the mechanism changed by the fix, and the regression results that support the conclusion.
References JDK 17: The jcmd Command JDK 17: Diagnostic Tools, JFR, and Native Memory Tracking JDK 17: Garbage-First Garbage Collector Tuning
description: Build an evidence chain from service symptoms to threads, JFR, garbage collection, and native memory in Java 17.
title: JVM Diagnostics: Separate CPU, Waiting, and Memory Before Tuning

content:
Scope: Java 17 CompletableFuture and the standard HttpClient. The code illustrates API composition rather than a complete production client.
Asynchronous calls avoid keeping a thread blocked for the entire operation, but resource costs remain. A request may have timed out at the API boundary while its underlying network operation continues. Retrying at that moment can leave the system doing two copies of the work.
Give the complete request one budget Suppose an incoming request has an 800-millisecond budget that includes validation, queueing, two external calls, and response assembly. Giving each external call its own 800-millisecond timeout can easily violate that overall commitment.
Calculate a deadline at ingress, use the remaining budget at each stage, and reserve time to return the response. Use a monotonic clock such as System.nanoTime() for elapsed time within a process. Cross-service propagation needs explicit protocol and clock-skew semantics; a process-local counter cannot simply be transmitted as a shared deadline.
Connection and request timeouts are also different. HttpClient’s connection timeout concerns establishing a new connection; it cannot be relied on to bound an entire request on a reused connection. HttpRequest’s timeout concerns waiting for a response. See HttpClient.Builder and HttpRequest.Builder . Streaming responses also need a deliberate read-deadline and resource-release policy.
A timed-out future does not prove the work stopped This fragment makes one GET request. Its types come from java.net, java.net.http, java.time, and java.util.concurrent:
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder() .connectTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(150)) .build(); // Reuse at service scope; do not create a client per request. HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder( URI.create("https://example.com/data")) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) .GET() .build(); CompletableFuture<String> result = client .sendAsync(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()) .thenApply(response -> { if (response.statusCode() != 200) { throw new CompletionException( new IllegalStateException("HTTP " + response.statusCode())); } return response.body(); }) .orTimeout(350, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); The 350-millisecond limit applies to the local future. It does not include time spent queueing before this fragment. orTimeout changes a future’s completion state; it does not promise to stop an arbitrary underlying operation. Likewise, CompletableFuture.cancel must not be assumed to interrupt the computation. See the CompletableFuture contract .
Observe both logical timeout and the actual release of network operations, connections, threads, and buffers. Once the caller has returned, late results must be discarded or handled according to an explicit policy; they cannot modify an already completed response.
Callback execution belongs in the design A callback without an Async suffix may execute on the thread completing the preceding stage. Heavy computation, synchronous I/O, or contended locking in that callback can delay the thread responsible for completing requests. Use an explicit, capacity-controlled executor for expensive work and monitor its queueing time.
Switching to thenApplyAsync does not automatically isolate dependencies. Async methods without an explicit executor may use the common pool, where one module’s blocking workload can affect others. Resource boundaries for different kinds of work should be visible in the implementation.
Before retrying, ask what a duplicate does A network timeout establishes that the caller did not receive a result in time. It does not establish that the server did nothing. Reads are often easier to retry. Writes such as charging a payment, creating an order, or appending a record need a stable idempotency key and server-side handling of the associated result. Generating a fresh key for each attempt defeats that protection.
Classify failures too. Invalid input usually requires an immediate failure. Rate limits require respecting the server’s pacing. Transient network failures may justify bounded retries. Backoff and jitter reduce synchronized retry spikes but do not create dependency capacity. See the AWS discussion of timeouts, retries, and jitter .
I express the policy with four limits: an overall deadline, a maximum attempt count, a per-attempt timeout, and a global retry budget. Stop when the next backoff plus a minimum useful execution time exceeds the remaining budget. Choose one layer to own retries; three attempts independently configured in the SDK, service wrapper, and entry point can multiply into unintended request amplification.
Validate the full lifecycle through failures Test delayed responses, connection failures, interrupted responses, rate limiting, and server success followed by a client timeout. Observe final error classification, actual attempt count, in-flight requests, and resource-recovery time. For writes, verify that the business effect occurs only once.
A dependable async client can explain why a call ended, whether underlying work is still running, whether a retry is safe, and how much of the total budget was consumed. A future completing quickly is only one part of that evidence.
References Java SE 17: CompletableFuture Java SE 17: HttpClient.Builder Java SE 17: HttpRequest.Builder AWS Builders’ Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
description: Separate CompletableFuture completion from the underlying request lifecycle, then constrain retries with deadlines, idempotency, and explicit budgets.
title: Java Async Calls: Timeouts, Cancellation, and Retries Are Separate Decisions

content:
An alert fires: consumer lag has been growing for ten minutes, but the job has not failed. Give the logs to a model and it may immediately suggest restarting the job. A restart can also invalidate caches, trigger replay, and increase the backlog. The engineering challenge is to turn evidence into verifiable actions.
This article uses a fictional streaming job. All thresholds are illustrative and do not describe a production system.
Define what the agent can decide A diagnostic workflow can have fixed stages: validate the alert, collect evidence, propose candidate causes, run inexpensive checks, and prepare a response plan. The model proposes the next useful hypothesis. Application code enforces identity, permissions, parameter validation, and execution budgets.
For example, “downstream writes are slow” needs supporting sink latency, error rates, retries, and upstream backpressure from the same time window. Consumer lag alone does not distinguish a traffic spike, partition skew, or resource contention. When evidence is missing, “not enough evidence to distinguish these causes” is more useful than presenting the most common cause as a fact.
Tools do not need to expose a general-purpose shell. Narrow interfaces such as get_job_metrics, get_recent_changes, and get_checkpoint_summary can constrain resource scope, time range, and response size. Treat raw logs as data to analyze. Commands appearing in a log must not automatically become execution instructions.
Make an action plan concrete An approval prompt that merely asks “Approve the optimization?” is insufficient. Bind approval to a specific target and parameters:
{ "plan_id": "incident-42-plan-2", "resource": "stream-job-demo", "action": "set_sink_concurrency", "before": 16, "after": 12, "expected_config_version": 8, "evidence": ["metric-snapshot-17", "change-record-9"], "observe_seconds": 300, "rollback_to": 16 } Reducing concurrency is a candidate response to an overloaded downstream service in this example, not a universal tuning recommendation. Before execution, verify that the target version is unchanged, health conditions still satisfy the preconditions, and approval has not expired. Changing the plan’s parameters invalidates the previous approval.
Amazon Bedrock’s return control mechanism hands a proposed action back to application code; user confirmation adds confirmation to selected actions. These are integration points. The execution service still needs to perform actual authorization checks. See Bedrock return control and user confirmation .
A timeout means an unknown outcome A particularly dangerous failure occurs when an action succeeds but its response is lost. The executor must not create a new operation ID merely because the request timed out.
execute(plan, operation_id): Validate the approved plan hash and the caller's permissions Atomically register operation_id; return its result if completed Read target configuration; check expected_config_version Call an idempotent control API using operation_id On timeout -> mark UNKNOWN -> inspect operation and target state Once confirmed -> persist the result and actual config version When the underlying API lacks idempotency, resource locks, conditional version updates, and an operation ledger can reduce risk. Some outcomes may still be impossible to resolve automatically. Escalate those for verification instead of asking a model to guess that the operation probably did not run.
A durable workflow does not guarantee that an external action executes only once. In LangGraph, resuming an interrupt restarts the interrupted node, including code before the interrupt. Side effects therefore need careful placement relative to approval waits. See LangGraph interrupts .
Rollback also has preconditions “Restore the previous concurrency” is safe only if this plan still owns the relevant change and nobody has subsequently modified the configuration. Condition rollback on the version returned by the successful action. If an operator has made a newer change, stop rather than overwrite it. Some operations, including message replay or state deletion, cannot be undone by reversing a parameter; the plan must define compensation or exclude automatic execution.
During observation, measure both benefits and side effects: is backlog growth slowing, is throughput recovering, and are failures or duplicate outputs increasing? A cleared alert is insufficient evidence; it may simply have been silenced. Save verification results in the incident record. Carry unresolved questions into follow-up tasks instead of recording an unverified procedure as successful.
Validate the entire workflow Start with five drills: actual downstream throttling, a burst of input, missing metrics, a lost execution response, and an operator changing configuration after approval. Check the diagnostic evidence, incorrect execution, duplicate execution, and detection of stale plans.
Measure at incident level: correctly diagnosed incidents divided by labeled incidents; plans requiring no additional evidence from an operator divided by all plans; executions without valid authorization; and incidents that recovered without a new failure divided by executed incidents. Measure recovery time from a consistent alert timestamp, separating human waiting, querying, and execution time. Otherwise, a process change can be mistaken for improved model capability.
An operations agent can first become reliable at collecting evidence and preparing plans, then gain access to narrowly scoped actions. Useful automation can explain why an action was needed, what actually happened, and how its effect was verified.
References Amazon Bedrock: Return control , application-controlled action execution. Amazon Bedrock: User confirmation , confirmation for selected actions. LangGraph: Interrupts , interruption, resumption, and node replay. The pseudocode here is framework-neutral; use the API of your pinned dependency version.
description: Design an auditable workflow for incident evidence, action plans, idempotent execution, and rollback verification.
title: Operations Agents: Separate Diagnosis, Approval, and Execution

content:
A user asks why yesterday’s conversion rate fell. A data agent generates SQL and reports an 8% decline. The task is not complete yet. Is the denominator clicks or impressions? Which time zone defines yesterday? Are conversions grouped by occurrence date or attributed click date? Has the data finished arriving?
A trustworthy data agent must access the right data, use the right metric definition, and connect its conclusions to concrete evidence. The model is one component of that query workflow.
Establish a query contract For an ambiguous question, consult a maintained metric catalog before creating a structured contract. An illustrative contract might be:
metric: attributed_order_cvr_v2 grain: campaign_id, business_date numerator: deduplicated attributed orders denominator: valid clicks date_basis: attributed click date timezone: Asia/Shanghai window: 2026-11-05 through 2026-11-06 freshness_requirement: partition completion status is ready Under this definition, conversion rate does not necessarily mean the probability that a clicking user places an order: one click may be associated with multiple orders. A user-probability metric needs a distinct-user numerator and a corresponding user denominator. The agent must preserve the agreed definition instead of silently changing it to simplify the SQL.
Fields outside the user’s authorized scope should not appear in the contract. A prompt saying “do not look at these fields” is not an access-control mechanism.
Enforce read-only behavior below the model The first layer is identity and data authorization: use a restricted identity appropriate to the task, authorized views, and necessary row and column restrictions. AWS Lake Formation supports row-, column-, and cell-level filtering, with limitations depending on the engine and data type. Validate the actual integration. See Lake Formation data filtering .
The second layer is a SQL gateway. Parse the entire syntax tree, permit only supported single queries and allowlisted functions, and recursively validate CTEs, subqueries, tables, and columns. Checking that the string starts with SELECT is insufficient: a dialect may allow file output, functions with side effects, or access to restricted system objects. Return structured rejection reasons so the model can make a bounded number of corrections.
The third layer is a resource budget: constrain date ranges, concurrency, runtime, output rows, and scanned bytes. LIMIT 100 generally limits returned rows and does not guarantee a small scan. Athena’s per-query scan limit can cancel an over-budget query. Workgroup aggregate thresholds primarily trigger alerts and should not be mistaken for an automatic hard stop. See Athena data usage controls .
Read-only means no changes to business source data; it does not mean no side effects. Queries incur costs and create audit logs and result files. Result storage still requires access controls and lifecycle management.
Attach provenance to results Joining fact tables at different grains can inflate metrics. The following illustrative SQL aggregates each side to the same grain before joining. It assumes orders have already been attributed and deduplicated:
WITH clicks AS ( SELECT campaign_id, attribution_date, COUNT(*) AS click_count FROM approved_valid_clicks WHERE attribution_date = :day GROUP BY campaign_id, attribution_date ), orders AS ( SELECT campaign_id, attribution_date, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count FROM approved_attributed_orders WHERE attribution_date = :day GROUP BY campaign_id, attribution_date ) SELECT c.campaign_id, c.click_count, COALESCE(o.order_count, 0) AS order_count, 1.0 * COALESCE(o.order_count, 0) / NULLIF(c.click_count, 0) AS cvr FROM clicks c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.campaign_id = o.campaign_id AND c.attribution_date = o.attribution_date; The left join retains click cohorts with no conversions. However, a key with attributed orders but no clicks is excluded, so a separate anti-join quality check is necessary. Return a query ID, SQL hash, parameters, metric version, data freshness, row count, and scanned bytes alongside the results. Numbers in the report should cite that query ID so the conclusion can be traced to the calculation.
Rule out definition changes before explaining a movement A useful validation order is partition completeness, agreement of base counts with a trusted report, join multiplication, stability of deduplication keys, and changes to dimension mappings. Only then inspect publisher or campaign breakdowns. Overall conversion rate is total orders divided by total clicks, not the unweighted average of group rates. A shift toward lower-converting groups can reduce the overall rate even if no group’s own rate falls.
“This group accounts for most of the decline” is a decomposition result. Without an experiment or another identification strategy, it does not establish that the group caused the decline. When evidence is insufficient, explain what is missing and propose the next query instead of inventing a definitive cause.
Acceptance cases should include zero denominators, late partitions, duplicate orders, time-zone boundaries, unauthorized fields, and excessive scans. Track numerical correctness, authorization enforcement, definition consistency, and correct abstention when the question cannot be answered. Compare result sets with appropriate tolerances instead of requiring identical SQL text: several queries may be equally valid.
References AWS Lake Formation: Data filtering and cell-level security , authorized data scope and integration limits. Amazon Athena: Data usage controls , per-query cancellation versus workgroup alerts. Anthropic: Demystifying evals for AI agents , validating environmental outcomes rather than the confidence of the answer.
